\chapter{Earth, Fire, Wind, Sky, Sea}
\label{ch:la-mundus}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the five great outdoor things in Latin and say which of them English inherited by descent and which it borrowed from books.}

The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[terra, terrae]{terra — dry land as opposed to sea, and the root under terrain, terrace and Mediterranean}

\label{lesson:LA-C45-terra}



\begin{quote}
A new group of five words begins here. Nothing is assumed but the alphabet you already read.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{terra} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the earth},\textquotedblright{} and specifically \textbf{dry land}.

That contrast is built into the word. \emph{Terra} is what is \textbf{not} sea — and the Romans named the Mediterranean on exactly that pattern, as \emph{the sea in the middle of the land}. You will have the second half of that name shortly, and when you do the whole thing stops being a proper noun and becomes a description you can read.

English took \emph{terra} freely: \textbf{terrain}, \textbf{terrestrial}, \textbf{subterranean}, a \textbf{terrace} (a raised bank of earth), and a \textbf{terrier} — a dog that goes to \textbf{ground} after its quarry. Even \textbf{inter}, to bury, is \emph{in} plus \emph{terra}: to put into the earth.

And \emph{terra firma}, \textquotedblleft{}solid ground,\textquotedblright{} is still said in Latin because no English phrase does the job as briefly.

English \textbf{earth} is Germanic and unrelated. Another coincidence worth naming rather than assuming.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{terra, terrae}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{terra} contrast with? (\textbf{The sea}.) So what does \textbf{Mediterranean} literally say? (\textbf{In the middle of the land}.) And what does it mean to \textbf{inter} someone? (To put them \textbf{into the earth}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ignis, ignis]{ignis — the classical word, which the Romance languages abandoned and English kept}

\label{lesson:LA-C45-ignis}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ignis} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fire}.\textquotedblright{}

This is Latin's own word, and it has a long pedigree: it is a genuine cousin of Sanskrit \textbf{agni}, the fire the Vedic hymns address, and of Russian \emph{ogon'}. Two of this book's tracks meet here, which is the point of having a Sanskrit track at all.

Now the strange part, and it is worth pausing on.

\textbf{No Romance language kept it.} French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese all threw \emph{ignis} away and built their word for fire on \emph{focus}, the hearth. The classical word for the commonest thing in the house simply lost.

But English kept it — as a \textbf{loan from books}. To \textbf{ignite} is to set on fire; \textbf{igneous} rock is rock that was once molten. So an English speaker saying \emph{ignite} is using Caesar's word for fire, while a Spanish speaker saying \emph{fuego} is not.

That is a good corrective to a natural assumption. \textbf{The daughter languages are not always the better guide to the parent.}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ignis, ignis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word did the Romance languages keep for fire — \emph{ignis} or \emph{focus}? (\emph{\textbf{Focus}}.) Which one did English borrow? (\emph{\textbf{Ignis}} — ignite, igneous.) And which Sanskrit word is its cousin? (\textbf{Agni}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ventus, ventī]{ventus — and a true Germanic cousin, with the sound change that proves it}

\label{lesson:LA-C45-ventus}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ventus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the wind}.\textquotedblright{}

Another \textbf{cousin}. Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}weh\textsubscript{1}-nto-}} gave Latin \emph{ventus} and Germanic \emph{windaz}, which is English \textbf{wind}. Latin's \emph{v} against English's \emph{w} is not a coincidence and not a corruption — it is regular, and once you have seen it you will see it everywhere.

The borrowed branch came later and from French: a \textbf{vent} is a hole for wind, to \textbf{ventilate} is to move wind through, and \textbf{ventilation} is what results.

And a \textbf{window} is a Norse gift, \emph{vindauga} — a \textbf{wind-eye}. The hole in the wall that the wind looks through. Even the Germanic side of the family named it after this word.

So English holds the same root three ways: inherited as \emph{wind}, borrowed as \emph{vent}, and compounded by the Vikings as \emph{window}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ventus, ventī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{wind} borrowed from \emph{ventus} or descended alongside it? (\textbf{Descended} — a cousin.) What regular difference marks the two branches? (Latin \textbf{v-}, Germanic \textbf{w-}.) And what does \emph{window} literally mean? (\textbf{Wind-eye}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[caelum, caelī]{caelum — the word under celestial, and under a ceiling painted like the sky}

\label{lesson:LA-C45-caelum}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{caelum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the sky},\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the heavens}.\textquotedblright{}

One word for both, which is why Latin can be ambiguous in exactly the places theology cares about. When a Roman said \emph{caelum}, the weather and the gods were the same place.

English took it directly as \textbf{celestial}, anything of the sky or the heavens, and in \textbf{Celeste} as a name. The blue called \emph{cerulean} is from the related \emph{caeruleus}, which you have already met as a colour.

\textbf{Ceiling} is very probably the same word, arriving through French — a vaulted ceiling in a great hall was painted to \emph{look} like sky, and the name stuck to the surface. The etymology is not perfectly settled, and this book will say so rather than round it off.

Two more you may already carry: the \textbf{equinox} you met with \emph{nox}, and \textbf{cyan}, which is Greek rather than Latin and arrived by its own road.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{caelum, caelī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things does \emph{caelum} name? (\textbf{The sky} and \textbf{the heavens}.) What is something \textbf{celestial}? (Of the sky.) And how confident is the \emph{ceiling} connection? (\textbf{Probable, not certain} — and the book says so.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mare, maris]{mare — the word that finishes Mediterranean and names every marine thing in English}

\label{lesson:LA-C45-mare}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mare} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the sea}.\textquotedblright{}

You met its partner a moment ago. \emph{Terra} is the land; \textbf{mare} is what is not land, and together they make the \textbf{mediterrāneum} — the sea in the middle of the earth. Two words you now hold explain a name most people use without reading.

The loans came thickly: \textbf{marine}, \textbf{maritime}, a \textbf{mariner}, a \textbf{submarine} (under the sea), and — through French — a \textbf{mermaid}, whose first half is this word.

And there is a cousin. Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*mori-}} also went down the Germanic road and gave English \textbf{mere}, an old word for a lake that survives in place names — Windermere, Grasmere. Small, standing water rather than an ocean, but the same ancestor.

So once again: a borrowed branch that sounds learned, and an inherited branch that sounds like a field in the north of England.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
